title: Egypt
body:
O.P.
I am in the preliminary stages of planning a family trip to Egypt, sometime in 2027. Will be 2 adults and a 10yo girl.
Draft itinerary • Cairo – 4 days • Luxor – 3 days • Aswan & Abu Simbel – 3 days • Hurghada – 3–4 days
Major highlights • Giza Plateau: Pyramids & Sphinx • Grand Egyptian Museum • Karnak & Luxor Temples • Valley of the Kings • Aswan & Philae • Abu Simbel
A search of the forums reveals some previous discussions on Egypt and inparticular visas, not a lot on things to do and see.
I am interested in getting feedback on how long to spend in each place as well as any tips on places that may not feature on the usual itineraries. We do like to explore and visit some of the less touristy places that cater for locals more so.
Has anyone got experience travelling self-guided rather than organised tours? We much prefer to move at our own pace, utilising private transport and guides as opposed to group tours; However, we also understand some places simply require tours to reach certain sites so keen to hear from personal experiences.
Will most likely be flying via Singapore or Malaysia and will spend a few nights, and I am trying to plan a quick visit to Qiddiya City, Riyadh to check out the newly opened Six Flags – It looks like its very achievable with direct flights from Cairo.
Any other guidance is always appreciated. We have time on our side and will tweak plans based on suggestions and further research. Ideal plan is to spend about ~15 days in Egypt although this is flexible.

I went on a guided tour in 2023 and I can't imagine doing a self guided tour. I would have missed so much.
STGM81 writes...
We much prefer to move at our own pace, utilising private transport and guides as opposed to group tours
You can still do that in a private guided tour. The Egyptian tour guides are very accommodating and knowledgeable. They will explain everything as you go along. My husband and I did a luxury guided tour for 9 days which cost about 750USD each which included tickets to the sites, accommodation at the Hyatt Regency in Cairo and he Hilton in Luxor, plane fares to Luxor and back to Cairo, a guide, air conditioned vehicle and driver. We were picked up at the airport and protected throughout. Everywhere you go, you have security, there are armed police points every kilometre or so and the hotels where we stayed had bomb sniffer dogs at the entrance. The hotels were gated.
There's so much more to Egypt than the sites you mentioned eg their oils and perfumes, rug making, potteries, silversmithing, churches, the market place, spices...
Valley of the Kings
I would add the valley of the queens and in particular Nefertari's tomb. The tomb is the absolute best. It's expensive to get into but very worth it. I have a video on my YouTube channel https://youtu.be/s_bwFU2kcj4?si=U8DDFCjaCKaezF7N
Grand Egyptian Museum
There's a new museum also, I'm not sure if it's open yet. But, wherever Tutankhamen is, head for that museum before opening time, wait for it to open and then head straight for that exhibit. You'll miss the crowds then. Everything else is secondary IMO and you can do comfortably and at leisure but in a room with Tutankhamen on your own is special. You're not allowed to photograph in that room so be aware of that.
I would also consider going to Alexandria on a day tour to the library.
I also used the app Find Penguins to record and track where we went.
Egypt has a tipping culture so be prepared for that. Our guide took care of it. I only had to tip when I went to the toilet.
As for the tombs, they get a bit monotonous after the first few. The exception is Nefertari's tomb. Our guide bribed the attendants and guards to let us in alone for longer than the 10 minutes allowed. Edit: there's a bit of "exchange" going on between the tour guides and the sites' attendants and guards so you'll gain that advantage as well.
Driving in Egypt... I would not consider it. Not for a minute. I would not even consider walking around.
[User #8158854370 postsYoung CodgerWhirlpool Forums Addict] I'm a self guided tour addict and had little trouble organising an Egypt tour. It's a little harder than some countries due to certain cities and areas being relatively closed to tourists. The other issue is touts but if you practice non engagement (something that does not come naturally to Westerners you'll be fine.) Tripadvisor has numerous helpful experts that can fill you in on the way to go. It's relatively simple as the "usual" spots are well travelled. Youtube is another resource. Your trip split (time wise) looks relatively leisurely. Allow quiet time in your hotel each day which helps counter the bustle of the streets. In Cairo I'd add the Citadel and the Coptic area. Also go downtown and try the local food. Entertaining a ten year old (other than in Hurghada) could be a challenge. Up to you but I'd be tempted to drop Aswan etc in favour of more beach days in Hurghada. Your idea of Riyadh is a good one Like cathedrals in Europe it's easy in Egypt to suffer from tomb/temple fatigue. Egypt is probably the last bastion of the organised tour but it is certainly doable. On guides I use wikipedia these days. The entries relating to the major sites are extremely detailed and easy to read on the spot or just before you enter a site.

Our 10yo (at time of travel), who is about to turn 9, has already travelled to 13 countries. So far, they have found museums, temples and history quite fascinating — probably more so than us ???? However, we all love roller coasters and have enjoyed plenty during our travels.
Egypt is probably the last bastion of the organised tour but it is certainly doable. On guides I use wikipedia these days. The entries relating to the major sites are extremely detailed and easy to read on the spot or just before you enter a site.
We are not anti-organised tours; we just find that we often want to spend longer at one place, and then another place will have an allocated time that is way too long for us. I am an amateur photographer, so what I want to see is not always the same as others. Being ‘free’ to do what we want and when has its benefits for us. A private guide would be the best compromise, although not always economical, so it’s a balance.
[User #398163637 postssuperbunnyWhirlpool Enthusiast] I would organise a flight from Cairo to Abu Simble return or Aswan as otherwise you will have to fly back to these places just to start your fight to Abu Simbel. Free travel around Egypt is great, you should have no problems if you respect the culture. I did hostels and other cheap hotels and arranged transportation to places through my accommodation. Don’t miss Valley of the Queens, Carters House and a balloon ride in Luxor. You’re going to miss some places as they can be hard to get to. Some simple Arabic words would be good to know such as no thank you and yes and water as your need plenty of that. Time of year should not be in their summer it will kill you, very hot. The shoulder months are good but I believe the best kept secret is winter as it’s very much cooler and virtually no rain with sunny sky’s. You will get pestered from sellers but that’s part of course. I went with my wife vis Bangkok and then flying Royal Jordan air, competitive price and good service. Egypt air not so good.

STGM81 writes...
Do you have any details of the guide or company that you used?
Yes, we used these people https://www.egypttoursportal.com/en-us/ chose a private tour and tweaked it. I was adamant on seeing Nefertari's tomb and Alexandria. I also wanted to see the light show at the Giza pyramids. While we were there, a government official turned up and it was a bit scary not knowing what was going on because our guide ensconced us and called for the car.
I was both fascinated and saddened by the people that live in cemeteries.
The guide talked with pride of the hospital and the free medical care but on driving past it, the streets were filled with people waiting for medical care.
Did you feel unsafe?
Other than the one time at the light show, never. The guide was with us all the time. The van and driver never far away. The driver always let us out on the footpath side. The only time we walked around streets was at the Khan Al-Khalili bazaar and outside the museum to enter it.
We used a different company to go to Alexandria and that driver let us out into traffic. That was a group tour but it was only 6 of us.
Young Codger writes...
add the Citadel and the Coptic area.
Both really worth going to. There was an old man in the Coptic area that cleaned shoes with passion. He was extremely happy when I paid him $10US. You'll need your shoe cleaned at some stage. IIRC he was near the hanging church. That was another area where we had to walk.
At Giza, you can go to the desert near the pyramids on quad bikes. We did that. Never again. Here again we had a guide. The back streets smelled awful but once we were in the open desert, it was better. I just didn't fancy bouncing around on a quad bike on desert sand. My husband enjoyed it.
Also, it appears the new museum is now open and that's where Tutankhamen resides. https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ckg4q403rpzo
The porters at the airport are something else too. The guides that picked us up and dropped us off wouldn't let us use them, but on departure, I ended up hiring one for tips and he carried all our suitcases and got us through the fast lane. So use your own judgment on that.
The women and men are separated at the security checkpoints. They have separate queues for women and children and the men. Don't fight it. Your wife and child will be within sight and the airport officials in the women's queues are women. IIRC we went through about 3 security checkpoints on departure.
At all the sites and hotels, there were checkpoints and all bags and us went through security scanners. The hotels we stayed at had the gate security to go through as well.
STGM81 writes...
We are not anti-organised tours; we just find that we often want to spend longer at one place, and then another place will have an allocated time that is way too long for us.
If we wanted to stay longer we stayed. If we weren't interested in something, we skipped it. It would have been different in a group tour but it was a private tour just for us.
superbunny writes...
Time of year should not be in their summer it will kill you, very hot.
We went in late May and it was starting to get hot then. Definitely take lots of water with you. You will need it. We're Queenslanders though. We arrived in Cairo from touring England and Ireland and I'll never do two hemispheres again because we had to dress for two climates which meant more luggage.
Edit: the Hatshepsut Temple was amazing and in Alexandria, we visited the catacombs.

After a weekend of more research and taking advice from the feedback received, our preliminary plans are as follows:
• Cairo – 4 Nights • Luxor – 4 Nights • Riyadh – 2 Nights • Sharm El-Sheikh – 6 Nights
As mentioned above, it looks like we will return via Cairo multiple times: Cairo -> Luxor -> Cairo -> Riyadh -> Cairo -> Sharm El-Sheikh -> Cairo and we may need to add an extra transit day if flight times aren't favourable.
Although I will keep an eye on direct flights between Riyadh & Sharm El-Sheikh and use that if it makes more sense to do so. Usually I don't like backtracking, but it does appear that it's a signicant saving to do so in this instance.

[User #905785708 postsWaldaWhirlpool Enthusiast] STGM81 writes...
Has anyone got experience travelling self-guided rather than organised tours?
Yeah i travelled there independently in March 2025. 3 Nights each in Cairo & Luxor, flights between the 2 with Air Egypt. There was nothing i missed out on by not doing a tour, in fact, it was the opposite.
Arriving at the Pyramids early i walked in and there was only a few other people at the gate, no crowds. Walked by myself out to the panoramic viewpoint, started to wonder if i was going the wrong place or would get yelled at by the police/security driving around since nobody else was there. By time i left the site, the buses had come in and everything was crowded.
Similar experience in Valley of the Kings Luxor. Arrived when they opened, did 3 tombs. 1st tomb was only 3 other people, i had to wait at the end for 15mins for someone to finally come down the bottom to ask them to take my photo. The 2nd tomb was literally just me (furthest from the entrance). Then by time i did these and walked back toward the entrance for the 3rd tomb, oh boy the crowds were insane! The tour buses had pulled in and there as now a line to get into the tomb. The entire time in the tomb was a line of people 1 step at a time, crammed in like sardines, couldn't wait to get out of there.
I did not enjoy that 3rd tomb at all. Then as i left it occurred to me, that for everyone on the tours, that was actually their only & entire experience of Egypt, completely unaware of the experience i just had of 2 empty tombs to myself. Same with the pyramids, and all the other temples etc. Crazy how they then come back telling everyone how great it is and to book a tour, guess they just don't know any better.
Anyways, Egypt like an country is possible & better going independently.

ctrl-alt-doll writes...
We were picked up at the airport and protected throughout. Everywhere you go, you have security, there are armed police points every kilometre or so and the hotels where we stayed had bomb sniffer dogs at the entrance. The hotels were gated.
An armed security guard (govt mandated at the time I think) rode on our bus and accompanied our tour group to each destination we went to.
One time, our luggage (the entire group's luggage) did not turn up at one airport. The airport baggage officials said it was 'delayed', and so we were also 'delayed' in leaving the airport.
After about 20 minutes and what appeared to be some conversation between the airport officials and our tour leader, he positioned himself alone in open space around the baggage pickup conveyors standing motionless with his hands behind his back. In one hand he held a roll of notes. After standing there for about a minute an airport official casually walked past and without any other interaction relived the tour leader of the money. Shortly after all our bags began rolling out on the pickup conveyor.
Later on I asked the tour leader what that was all about. I think he was a bit disturbed it had actually been observed by anyone in the group. He denied he paid a bribe, instead putting the delay incident down to confusion over who exactly was to provide a security guard for the group's bus to enable it to leave the airport.
[User #6562511379 postsThuddWorld peace through beerWhirlpool Forums Addict] STGM81 writes...
Has anyone got experience travelling self-guided rather than organised tours?
I've done Egypt entirely self-guided. It is certainly possible, and probably preferable in many cases simply because you don't arrive somewhere just as a dozen other buses do.
The closest we came to an organised tour was hiring a driver for the day to take as to Saqqara and the Red Pyramid (the bent pyramid was closed at the time). Apart from a bored guard we were the only people there.
We are actually considering skipping Aswan & Abu Simbel now.
I loved Aswan. The Nile is particularly beautfiul down there over the cascades. Exploring the Nubian villiage was fascinating. Visited some digs on the 'other' side of the river. Loved exploring Philae, the town souks and the riverside restaurants. Splurged and stayed in the magnificent Old Cataract hotel (where Agatha Christie wrote 'Death on the Nile'). Abu Simbel was amazing – we flew there, then I got off the plane and dashed down to be first there and got a set of photos with nobody else in them. We took the sleeper train from Luxor and it was a fun journey.
STGM81 writes...
Grand Egyptian Museum
Admittedly I like this stuff, but I went to what was at the time the old museum three times – twice to get around everything, and then another visit to see Tutankhamun's gold one more time.
places that may not feature on the usual itineraries
We wandered [deliberately] into the Khan El-Khalili Bazaar without a map. Spent the afternoon wandering through the maze of alleys and exploring strange little shops. We stumbled across one of the last remaining traditional fez makers in the market and I had one made. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KYPXGqtacpw
Valley of the Kings Tip: buy two tickets. Each ticket gets you into three tombs (Tut's tomb and a couple of others have their own separate tickets), and that can be over surprisingly quckly. You'll never be there again, so get a second ticket to visit additional tombs.
We also arranged to go to the tomb of Ay, a fascinating tomb a little bit out of the way that few people visit. You may have to arrange for it to be opened – sometimes there is a guard there who will unlock it, we had to have someone with a key come with us.
Tombs of the Nobles are also a must-see IMO.
Any other guidance is always appreciated. In Luxor, you simply must go here. I cannot stress this enough. Preferably in the evening for the views across the Nile to Karnak. One of the best meals I've had in my life . https://www.tripadviso r.com.au/Restaurant_Review-g 294205-d1996015-Reviews-Tuta nkhamon-Luxor_Nile_River_Valley.html

The company had option for "Driver only" which i used.
